SAFE (SIMPLE AGREEMENT FOR FUTURE EQUITY) NOTE
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

INVESTMENT AMOUNT, VALUATION CAP, AND DISCOUNT RATE
Jordan Morgan agrees to pay Acme, Inc. the amount of $50,000 (the "Purchase Amount") in exchange for this SAFE. Two of the terms most commonly negotiated in SAFEs are a valuation cap and a discount rate, either or both of which may apply to a given SAFE. A valuation cap sets a maximum company valuation, of $8,000,000, used to calculate the number or price of shares Jordan Morgan receives on conversion, so that Jordan Morgan converts as though Acme, Inc. had been valued at no more than the cap even if the actual financing round values the company higher. A discount rate, of 20%, gives Jordan Morgan the right to convert at a price equal to that percentage discount off the price paid by investors in the triggering equity financing round. Where both a cap and a discount apply, a SAFE commonly converts at whichever of the two produces the lower conversion price, unless the parties' agreement states otherwise. These are contractual deal terms negotiated between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Morgan; no statute or regulation defines or requires a valuation cap or a discount rate — these are private contract terms popularized by market practice (originating with Y Combinator's standard SAFE form), not creatures of statute.

CONVERSION TRIGGER — NEXT EQUITY FINANCING
This SAFE converts into shares of Acme, Inc.'s capital stock upon the closing of Acme, Inc.'s next "Equity Financing" — generally understood as the next transaction, or series of related transactions, in which Acme, Inc. issues and sells preferred stock for the principal purpose of raising capital, with a minimum aggregate gross proceeds threshold of $1,000,000 (typically excluding the conversion of SAFEs, convertible notes, or other convertible securities from that threshold, unless the parties agree otherwise). Acme, Inc. and Jordan Morgan may separately define whether a change of control, an initial public offering, or a dissolution of Acme, Inc. independently triggers payment or conversion on terms other than those applicable to an Equity Financing: On a Change of Control, this SAFE converts into the right to receive a cash payment equal to the greater of the Purchase Amount or the as-converted value of the SAFE.

MOST FAVORED NATION PROVISION
If, after the date of this SAFE and before it terminates (by conversion, payment, or otherwise), Acme, Inc. issues another SAFE, convertible note, or similar convertible security to any other investor on terms materially more favorable to that other investor than the terms of this SAFE — for example, a lower valuation cap, a larger discount rate, or additional investor rights — Acme, Inc. will provide Jordan Morgan notice of those terms, and Jordan Morgan will have the option to amend this SAFE to include the more favorable term(s), subject to the following conditions, deadlines, or exceptions: This provision terminates upon the closing of the next Equity Financing. This is a negotiated contractual protection, not a right created by statute or regulation.

FEDERAL REGISTRATION REQUIREMENT FOR SECURITIES OFFERINGS
A SAFE issued by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Morgan in exchange for cash is a security for purposes of federal securities law, because a SAFE conveys a contractual right to receive equity (or other consideration) in Acme, Inc. based on the future performance of Acme, Inc.'s business and the efforts of others. Section 5 of the Securities Act, codified at 15 U.S.C. § 77e, makes it unlawful to offer or sell a security using the mails or interstate commerce unless a registration statement is in effect, or has been filed, as to that security, or unless an exemption from registration applies. This registration requirement is a matter of federal law and applies uniformly regardless of which state the parties are located in.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Sale or delivery after sale of unregistered securities Unless a registration statement is in effect as to a security, it shall be unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly— (1) to make use of any means or instruments of transportation or communication in interstate commerce or of the mails to sell such security through the use or medium of any prospectus or otherwise; or (2) to carry or cause to be carried through the mails or in interstate commerce, by any means or instruments of transportation, any such security for the purpose of sale or for delivery after sale. ... (c) Necessity of filing registration statement It shall be unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly, to make use of any means or instruments of transportation or communication in interstate commerce or of the mails to offer to sell or offer to buy through the use or medium of any prospectus or otherwise any security, unless a registration statement has been filed as to such security, or while the registration statement is the subject of a refusal order or stop order or (prior to the effective date of the registration statement) any public proceeding or examination under section 77h of this title."
  — Securities Act of 1933, § 5, 15 U.S.C. § 77e(a), (c) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/77e)
  Known gap: Federal law does not automatically exempt a SAFE from registration merely because it is denominated as a contract rather than as "stock" or a "bond." Whether a particular SAFE offering may proceed without SEC registration depends on whether the offering qualifies for a registration exemption, addressed elsewhere in this document. This clause states the general registration requirement only; it does not identify which exemption, if any, applies to a specific offering, and does not constitute a determination that any exemption is available. This is a single statutory section (§ 5, 15 U.S.C. § 77e); no additional independent source was found for this.

REGULATION D RULE 506 PRIVATE OFFERING EXEMPTION — 506(B) VS. 506(C)
The most commonly used exemption from Securities Act registration for a SAFE offering by an early-stage company such as Acme, Inc. is Rule 506 of Regulation D, 17 C.F.R. § 230.506, which has two alternative tracks with materially different conditions. Under Rule 506(b), an issuer may sell to an unlimited number of accredited investors and up to 35 non-accredited investors who (individually or with a purchaser representative) have sufficient knowledge and experience to evaluate the investment, but the issuer and anyone acting on its behalf may not use general solicitation or general advertising to offer the securities. Under Rule 506(c), an issuer may use general solicitation and general advertising, but every purchaser in the offering must be an accredited investor, and the issuer must take reasonable steps to verify each purchaser's accredited-investor status rather than relying on the purchaser's self-certification alone. An offering under either track is exempt from Securities Act registration but is not exempt from the antifraud provisions of federal or state securities law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) Conditions to be met in offerings subject to limitation on manner of offering—(1) General conditions. To qualify for an exemption under this section, offers and sales must satisfy all the terms and conditions of §§ 230.501 and 230.502. (2) Specific conditions— (i) Limitation on number of purchasers. There are no more than, or the issuer reasonably believes that there are no more than, 35 purchasers of securities from the issuer in offerings under this section in any 90-calendar-day period. ... (ii) Nature of purchasers. Each purchaser who is not an accredited investor either alone or with his purchaser representative(s) has such knowledge and experience in financial and business matters that he is capable of evaluating the merits and risks of the prospective investment, or the issuer reasonably believes immediately prior to making any sale that such purchaser comes within this description."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(b), Regulation D, conditions in offerings subject to limitation on manner of offering (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.506)
  "(c) Conditions to be met in offerings not subject to limitation on manner of offering—(1) General conditions. To qualify for exemption under this section, sales must satisfy all the terms and conditions of §§ 230.501 and 230.502(a) and (d). (2) Specific conditions—(i) Nature of purchasers. All purchasers of securities sold in any offering under paragraph (c) of this section are accredited investors. (ii) Verification of accredited investor status. The issuer shall take reasonable steps to verify that purchasers of securities sold in any offering under paragraph (c) of this section are accredited investors."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(c), Regulation D, conditions in offerings not subject to limitation on manner of offering (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.506)
  "(c) Limitation on manner of offering. Except as provided in § 230.504(b)(1) or § 230.506(c), neither the issuer nor any person acting on its behalf shall offer or sell the securities by any form of general solicitation or general advertising, including, but not limited to, the following: (1) Any advertisement, article, notice or other communication published in any newspaper, magazine, or similar media or broadcast over television or radio; and (2) Any seminar or meeting whose attendees have been invited by any general solicitation or general advertising..."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.502(c), Regulation D, limitation on manner of offering (general-solicitation prohibition) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.502)
  Known gap: 506(b) and 506(c) are two alternative compliance paths within the same rule, not independently arising legal tracks — they are subsections of one regulation. The general-solicitation prohibition described above is stated in a related section of the same regulatory framework (Rule 502(c)), which Rule 506(b) incorporates by reference; it is not a source of law independent from Regulation D. Which track, if either, a particular offering satisfies depends on facts not stated here: whether general solicitation was used, how many purchasers participated and whether they are accredited, and what steps (if any) were taken to verify accredited status. This clause does not state that any specific offering qualifies for either track. This is a single regulatory framework (Regulation D, §§ 230.506, 230.502); no additional independent source was found for this.

DEFINITION OF "ACCREDITED INVESTOR"
Both tracks of the Rule 506 exemption depend in part on which purchasers qualify as "accredited investors," a term defined by SEC rule at 17 C.F.R. § 230.501(a). The definition includes, among other categories, natural persons whose individual net worth (or joint net worth with a spouse or spousal equivalent) exceeds $1,000,000, excluding the value of the person's primary residence; natural persons with individual income exceeding $200,000 (or joint income with a spouse or spousal equivalent exceeding $300,000) in each of the two most recent years with a reasonable expectation of reaching the same level in the current year; and certain institutional and entity purchasers. The definition was amended in 2020 to add further categories, including natural persons holding certain professional certifications, designations, or credentials that the SEC has specifically recognized as qualifying a person for accredited-investor status, and "knowledgeable employees" of certain private funds. The definition below is the current version, last amended effective February 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Accredited investor. Accredited investor shall mean any person who comes within any of the following categories, or who the issuer reasonably believes comes within any of the following categories, at the time of the sale of the securities to that person: ... (5) Any natural person whose individual net worth, or joint net worth with that person's spouse or spousal equivalent, exceeds $1,000,000; ... (6) Any natural person who had an individual income in excess of $200,000 in each of the two most recent years or joint income with that person's spouse or spousal equivalent in excess of $300,000 in each of those years and has a reasonable expectation of reaching the same income level in the current year; ... (10) Any natural person holding in good standing one or more professional certifications or designations or credentials from an accredited educational institution that the Commission has designated as qualifying an individual for accredited investor status. ..."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.501(a), Regulation D, accredited investor definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.501)
  Known gap: Whether a particular investor meets any category of this definition depends on facts about that investor's income, net worth, professional credentials, or institutional status that are outside the scope of this document. The list of SEC-recognized professional certifications referenced in the rule is maintained separately by the SEC and is not reproduced here. This is a single regulatory subsection (17 C.F.R. § 230.501(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

CALIFORNIA NOTICE FILING FOR FEDERALLY COVERED RULE 506 OFFERINGS
State securities law applies independently of federal securities law; qualifying for a federal registration exemption such as Rule 506 does not by itself satisfy state-law requirements. However, the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 amended the federal Securities Act to preempt states from imposing their own registration or qualification requirements on securities offered under SEC rules issued pursuant to Securities Act § 4(2) (the private-offering exemption under which Regulation D, including Rule 506, was adopted), while expressly preserving state authority to impose a notice filing requirement substantially similar to the one in effect on September 1, 1996. California's Corporations Code implements this framework: for an offer or sale exempt from federal registration under Rule 506, California requires a notice filing with the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation — in the form of a copy of the Form D filed with the SEC — within 15 days of the first sale in California, together with a consent to service of process and payment of a notice filing fee. This obligation is separate from, and additional to, compliance with the federal exemption; it is specific to California, and other states may impose different notice-filing or fee requirements for the same offering.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(d) Any offer or sale of a security with respect to a transaction that is exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933 pursuant to Section 18 (b)(4)(F) of that act, if all of the following requirements are met: (1) A notice in the form of a copy of the completed Form D (17 C.F.R. 239.500) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission is filed with the commissioner within 15 days of the first sale in this state, along with documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in annual or periodic reports that the commissioner by rule or order deems appropriate. The commissioner may allow for a notice in the form of the electronic transmission of the information in Form D. (2) A consent to service of process under Section 25165 is filed with the notice as required by paragraph (1). (3) Payment of the notice filing fee provided for in subdivision (c) of Section 25608.1 is made."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102.1(d), California Corporations Code, notice filing exemption from qualification for federally covered securities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.1)
  "(F) Commission rules or regulations issued under section 77d(2) of this title, except that this subparagraph does not prohibit a State from imposing notice filing requirements that are substantially similar to those required by rule or regulation under section 77d(2) of this title that are in effect on September 1, 1996; or"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 77r(b)(4)(F), NSMIA federal preemption of state registration for Rule 506-type offerings, preserving notice-filing authority (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/77r)
  Known gap: Whether California's notice filing requirement applies to a particular offering, and the precise fee amount and filing mechanics currently in effect, depend on facts about the offering — including whether any California resident purchases the security — that are outside the scope of this document.

ANTIFRAUD LIABILITY APPLIES REGARDLESS OF REGISTRATION EXEMPTION
Qualifying for an exemption from registration, whether under Rule 506 or any other exemption, does not exempt an offer or sale of a SAFE from the antifraud provisions of federal or California securities law. At the federal level, Section 17(a) of the Securities Act makes it unlawful, in the offer or sale of any security, to employ any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud; to obtain money or property by means of an untrue statement of a material fact or an omission of a material fact necessary to make the statements made not misleading; or to engage in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit on the purchaser. California law contains an independent, parallel prohibition: it is unlawful for any person to offer or sell (or buy or offer to buy) a security in California by means of a written or oral communication that includes an untrue statement of a material fact or omits a material fact necessary to make the statements made not misleading.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Use of interstate commerce for purpose of fraud or deceit It shall be unlawful for any person in the offer or sale of any securities (including security-based swaps) or any security-based swap agreement (as defined in section 78c(a)(78) of this title) by the use of any means or instruments of transportation or communication in interstate commerce or by use of the mails, directly or indirectly— (1) to employ any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud, or (2) to obtain money or property by means of any untrue statement of a material fact or any omission to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, in light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading; or (3) to engage in any transaction, practice, or course of business which operates or would operate as a fraud or deceit upon the purchaser."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 77q(a), Securities Act of 1933 § 17(a), fraudulent interstate transactions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/77q)
  "It is unlawful for any person to offer or sell a security in this state, or to buy or offer to buy a security in this state, by means of any written or oral communication that includes an untrue statement of a material fact or omits to state a material fact necessary to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which the statements were made, not misleading."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25401, California Corporate Securities Law, fraud in issuance, purchase, or sale of security (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25401)
  Known gap: This clause states the existence and general terms of these antifraud provisions; it does not evaluate whether any particular statement made, or omitted, in connection with a specific offering would violate them. Other antifraud provisions exist at both the federal level (including Exchange Act Rule 10b-5) and under California law that are not quoted here.

At the federal level, Section 17(a) of the Securities Act makes it unlawful, in the offer or sale of any security, to employ any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud; to obtain money or property by means of an untrue statement of a material fact or an omission of a material fact necessary to make the statements made not misleading; or to engage in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit on the purchaser. California law contains an independent, parallel prohibition: it is unlawful for any person to offer or sell (or buy or offer to buy) a security in California by means of a written or oral communication that includes an untrue statement of a material fact or omits a material fact necessary to make the statements made not misleading.

citations.cite: Securities Act of 1933 § 17(a), fraudulent interstate transactions
citations.quote: (a) Use of interstate commerce for purpose of fraud or deceit It shall be unlawful for any person in the offer or sale of any securities (including security-based swaps) or any security-based swap agreement (as defined in section 78c(a)(78) of this title) by the use of any means or instruments of transportation or communication in interstate commerce or by use of the mails, directly or indirectly— (1) to employ any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud, or (2) to obtain money or property by means of any untrue statement of a material fact or any omission to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, in light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading; or (3) to engage in any transaction, practice, or course of business which operates or would operate as a fraud or deceit upon the purchaser.

citations.cite: California Corporate Securities Law, fraud in issuance, purchase, or sale of security
citations.quote: It is unlawful for any person to offer or sell a security in this state, or to buy or offer to buy a security in this state, by means of any written or oral communication that includes an untrue statement of a material fact or omits to state a material fact necessary to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which the statements were made, not misleading.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the existence and general terms of these antifraud provisions; it does not evaluate whether any particular statement made, or omitted, in connection with a specific offering would violate them. Other antifraud provisions exist at both the federal level (including Exchange Act Rule 10b-5) and under California law that are not quoted here.
